text: Saying an incident is eradicated because a scan came back clean isn't enough. Real eradication is three separate jobs: remove the attacker's active tooling, close the vulnerability that let them in, and remove everything they planted while inside, built specifically to outlast a cleanup. Skip any one of the three and the incident doesn't actually go away — it just hides until it resurfaces, often weeks later.

Meridian Outpatient Billing's root cause was an internet-facing Remote Desktop Gateway missing a critical update for weeks. From there the attacker planted three separate footholds in case one was found: a rogue local admin account, svc-helpdesk, a scheduled task that relaunched a PowerShell-based payload on every reboot, and a registry Run key on a billing clerk's workstation. Containment isolated the servers from the network — it never cleaned a single one of them.

Get-ScheduledTask confirms what SystemHealthCheck actually runs before anyone touches it — deleting blind risks removing a legitimate scheduled job by mistake, which is its own kind of self-inflicted outage. Once it's confirmed as the attacker's, Unregister-ScheduledTask -Confirm:$false removes it outright, with the switch skipping the interactive confirmation prompt.

The rogue account and the registry entry come out the same way: confirm first, then remove. Get-LocalUser and Get-ItemProperty show exactly what's sitting there before anything changes; Remove-LocalUser and Remove-ItemProperty take each one out cleanly. Same verify-then-remove pattern every single time, regardless of what kind of persistence it is.

Account creation and new scheduled tasks both leave event log entries behind — Event ID 4720 and Event ID 4698. Meridian's team checks both across every host in scope, not just the one host where the first foothold happened to be spotted, because a fourth, undiscovered one could easily be sitting somewhere else in the environment, waiting.

None of that cleanup matters if the Gateway server itself stays unpatched — that's how the attacker actually got in, and it's exactly as open today as it was before any of this cleanup started. Eradication only finishes once the tooling is gone, every foothold is verified removed on every affected host, and the root-cause vulnerability has genuinely been closed.
